clue.text: Party yawning loudly, part of the furniture

parts.note: a side is a party or faction in a dispute

indicators.note: loudly says the word for yawning is to be heard spoken, not read

parts.note: yawning from tedium means being bored

explanation.surface: Someone at a dull party yawns noisily while slumped against the furniture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'loudly' signals that BORED is taken by its sound, giving the spelling BOARD.
explanation.definitionFit: A sideboard is a long cabinet for a dining room, a familiar item of furniture.

clue.text: See 21
See 22
Attempt to outline exercise for a man, perhaps?

indicators.note: to outline something is to go round its edge, so the attempt surrounds the exercise

parts.note: a bid is an attempt at something
PE is physical education, school exercise

explanation.surface: Someone tries to sketch out a workout routine suitable for a man.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a man, perhaps?' signals an example: any two-legged creature fits, man being one.
explanation.definitionFit: Any two-legged animal is a biped, and a man is one example, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Current measurer a short distance above tree, adjusted

indicators.note: in a down clue, above means the first pieces sit over the next in the column

parts.note: MM is a millimetre, a very short distance

indicators.note: adjusted means the letters of tree are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An electrician's meter is fixed a little way up a tree and tweaked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'adjusted' turns TREE into ETER, placed below A and MM in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: An ammeter is the instrument that measures electrical current in amperes.

clue.text: Dropped dead? That's about right

indicators.note: about means going around, so dead surrounds the right

parts.note: deceased is a formal word for dead

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a fallen figure has died, and gets the reply that this is roughly correct.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' puts R inside DECEASED.
explanation.definitionFit: Dropped in the sense of fell or lessened, as in a price going down.

clue.text: Run away, seeing wolf

definitions.meaning: to wolf food is to gulp it

explanation.surface: Someone flees on catching sight of a wolf.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are standard verbs: flee in a hurry, and swallow food too fast.

clue.text: Rear jetty going less smoothly

parts.note: bum is informal British for the backside
a pier is a jetty projecting into the sea

explanation.surface: Someone backs up a jetty while the ride gets rougher.
explanation.definitionFit: A bumpier ride or road is a rougher one, with more jolts and less smooth progress.

clue.text: Richard I — or IO?

parts.note: the letters IO are the middle, or heart, of the word lion

explanation.surface: A puzzle over whether a king's name could be written as just two letters.
explanation.walkthrough: IO looks like the moon of Jupiter or a Roman numeral echo of Richard I, but it is the heart of LION.
explanation.definitionFit: King Richard I of England was nicknamed the Lionheart, Coeur de Lion, for his courage.

clue.text: Gorilla heading for zoo held by girl from behind — appearing calmer?

indicators.note: from behind means the whole build is read backwards
held by means the girl contains the gorilla and zoo letter

parts.note: a maid is an old word for a girl
a gorilla is a great ape

indicators.note: heading for points to the first letter of zoo

explanation.surface: A girl carrying a gorilla away to the zoo seems to grow more relaxed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'held by' and 'from behind' work together: the gorilla and Z go inside the girl, then the whole run is read backwards to give the drug.
explanation.definitionFit: Diazepam (Valium) is a sedative drug, a calmer in the sense of something that soothes anxiety.

clue.text: Mundane as Wimbledon, perhaps?

definitions.meaning: Wimbledon ... is an open ... in south-west London

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether Wimbledon counts as ordinary.
explanation.walkthrough: Wimbledon suggests tennis, but the second reading is Wimbledon Common, a public open space in London.
explanation.definitionFit: Something commonplace is ordinary and unremarkable, the same as mundane.

clue.text: Frozen, grabbing last of heat, as cold

indicators.note: grabbing means the first word takes hold of the letter, putting it inside

parts.note: a frozen liquid has become solid

indicators.note: last of points to the final letter of heat

explanation.surface: Something frozen clutches at the last bit of warmth, still as cold as ever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'grabbing' puts T inside SOLID.
explanation.definitionFit: A stolid person is impassive and unemotional, cold in manner.

clue.text: Privilege claimed by Americans with their sleeves rolled up, they say?

indicators.note: they say means the phrase is taken as it sounds when spoken

parts.note: rolled-up sleeves leave the forearms uncovered, which is having the freedom to show bare forearms

explanation.surface: Americans in shirtsleeves claim a liberty, so people report.
explanation.walkthrough: 'they say' means the bare-arms phrase is heard, and BARE sounds like BEAR, the carrying of weapons.
explanation.definitionFit: The Second Amendment to the US Constitution protects citizens' freedom to keep and carry weapons.

clue.text: Paul forbidding fish

parts.note: Paul is the setter, so the setter refers to himself as me
forbidding in the sense of stern and grim-looking

explanation.surface: Paul is banning something to do with fish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'forbidding' looks like a verb, but it is an adjective meaning grim.
explanation.definitionFit: The megrim is a flatfish of European waters, related to the turbot.

clue.text: Try getting goal, English support lacking at first

parts.note: an end is an aim or goal

indicators.note: lacking at first means the opening letter is removed

parts.note: to favour someone is to support them

explanation.surface: A footballer tries to score while the English backing falters early.
explanation.walkthrough: 'lacking at first' drops F from FAVOUR, leaving AVOUR.
explanation.definitionFit: To endeavour is to try hard, and an endeavour is an attempt.

clue.text: Sully spirit measure I'm to serve up, small amount

indicators.note: in a down clue, serve up means the whole build reads upward, reversed

parts.note: to mar is to spoil or sully
a gill is a small liquid measure used for spirits
taken as written without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Someone serves a tainted shot of spirits, admitting a small measure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to serve up' reverses MARGILLIM in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A milligram is a thousandth of a gram, a tiny quantity of weight.

clue.text: Indian dress in chestnut and white — perhaps one cultivating flowers

indicators.note: in means the dress is placed inside the horse colour

parts.note: a roan horse has a coat of a base colour such as chestnut mixed with white hairs
a sari is the wrapped garment worn by Indian women

explanation.surface: A woman in a chestnut and white sari tends her flower garden.
explanation.walkthrough: ROAN is a horse coat colour: a base such as chestnut flecked with white hairs.
explanation.definitionFit: A rosarian is a rose grower or enthusiast, so one example of a flower cultivator.

clue.text: Characters 1, 3 and 5 in an over?

definitions.meaning: characters in the sense of eccentric people
a cricket over has six deliveries; the first, third and fifth are the odd-numbered balls

explanation.surface: Someone lists the characters numbered one, three and five in a cricket over.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket an over is a set of six balls bowled by one bowler.
explanation.definitionFit: Eccentric people are called characters or oddballs.

clue.text: Idiotic dropping in without support

indicators.note: dropping means the word that follows is taken away

parts.note: brainless means foolish or idiotic
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fool drops in unsupported.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dropping in' looks like visiting, but it removes IN from BRAINLESS.
explanation.definitionFit: Going braless means wearing no bra, the garment of support.

clue.text: Defamation's left in a lower position for actor Adam

indicators.note: in a lower position means the letter is shifted further down this down entry

parts.note: slander is spoken defamation

explanation.surface: A Hollywood actor is demoted after a libel case.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in a lower position' moves the L of SLANDER down three places.
explanation.definitionFit: Adam Sandler is an American comic film actor.

clue.text: Talk with creature of the night in river

indicators.note: in means the creature goes inside the river

parts.note: the Dee is a river in Britain
a bat is a nocturnal creature

explanation.surface: A conversation with a bat flying over a river.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dee is a favourite crossword river, flowing through Wales, England and Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: A debate is a formal discussion, so talk in the noun or verb sense.

clue.text: Large short, drinking last of Havana Club, perhaps — this it?

definitions.text: Large short, drinking last of Havana Club, perhaps — this it?

indicators.note: drinking means the first part takes in the following letters
short means the word loses its final letter

parts.note: big means large

indicators.note: last of points to the final letter of Havana

parts.note: a club is one suit of playing cards, so a card

explanation.surface: A large tot of Havana Club rum is drunk, and someone wonders if this is the brand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'short' trims the last letter; 'drinking' takes the A of Havana and the card inside. Havana Club is a rival rum, so the whole clue points at the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Bacardi is a well-known brand of white rum, originally from Cuba like Havana Club.

clue.text: With an Irish accent and, initially, slurring it's dreadfully loud?

indicators.note: slurring speech runs its sounds together, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: initially points to the first letter of each of the next two words

explanation.surface: Someone with an Irish accent and slurring speech is extremely noisy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'initially' takes A from accent and A from and; 'slurring' rearranges them with WITHANIRISH.
explanation.definitionFit: A gaudy floral shirt is called loud, and these garish prints are a byword for loud clothing.

clue.text: Company of writers last to inscribe a final note, showing muscle

parts.note: Bic is a company that makes ballpoint pens, writing instruments

indicators.note: last to points to the final letter of inscribe

parts.note: PS is a postscript, a note added at the end of a letter

explanation.surface: A firm of authors adds a postscript to show its strength.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Company of writers' suggests a publisher, but writers here are pens.
explanation.definitionFit: The biceps is the large muscle at the front of the upper arm.

clue.text: Excellent thing, a light shone in a policeman's face?

definitions.meaning: something outstanding or showy, an informal British phrase

definitions.text: a light shone in a policeman's face?
definitions.meaning: a British policeman, and a ... is a bright light that blinds

explanation.surface: Someone praises a torch beam shone into a police officer's eyes.
explanation.walkthrough: BOBBY is British slang for a police officer.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is informal British and Australian slang for something or someone remarkably impressive.

clue.text: See 9
See 11
Party with fury rejected an African

parts.note: Lib is short for the Liberal party

indicators.note: rejected means turned back, so the word for fury is reversed

parts.note: ire is anger or fury
taken as written

explanation.surface: A political party furiously turns away an African.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rejected' turns IRE into ERI.
explanation.definitionFit: A Liberian is a person from Liberia in West Africa.

clue.text: See 11
Sacrifice armies and try to renegotiate

indicators.note: renegotiating terms means rearranging them, so the letters are shuffled

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Generals offer up troops and try to reopen peace talks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to renegotiate' rearranges ARMIES and TRY.
explanation.definitionFit: To martyrise someone is to make a martyr of them, putting them to death for a cause.
